transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-15
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~64 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Arjun Rao (CTO - Lytic), Mei Lin (SRE Lead - Lytic), Sofia Patel (PM - Lytic)
Shared links: demo deck (drive.redwood/demo-lytic), sample benchmark repo (github.com/redwood/benchmarks/sample-k6)

-- Optional auto-generated summary (may be imperfect) --
Quick notes: walked through console rate settings, shown API examples for org/project key headers, demoed a simulated burst and fallback to lower-cost model; covered KMS and audit log options.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we're gonna run through how Redwood handles tenant-level rate controls and, uh, priority slices. diego and i will tag team.
[00:12] Arjun: thanks, Maya. quick thing, we have a noisy weekend batch that spikes CPU usage, so our main ask is how to let prod traffic burst but not kill other teams.
[00:22] Diego: yup that's exactly why we've got the 'burst slice' and leaky-bucket profiles, you can set a steady leak rate plus a bucket capacity so short spikes are absorbed without dropping.
[00:35] Mei: little clarifying question - how does that interact with org vs project keys? we use org keys for infra calls and project keys for customer facing, want to isolate them.
[00:47] Maya: great Q. you can attach quotas at both levels — org level provides a floor and global control, project keys can have their own concurrency caps and burst allowances. typical pattern is org quota to enforce company-wide monthly cap and project keys to do per-product throttles.
[01:05] Sofia: and what about sticky routing? we don't want a high-cost model to be used for low-priority events.
[01:12] Diego: we demoed policy routing — you define priority rules, e.g., header X-tenant-priority: high, and that routes to dedicated pool or higher-priced model. fallback policy sends to cheaper quantized variant when dedup or capacity breach happens.
[01:28] Arjun: ok makes sense. in practice, if two projects spike simultaneously, what decides who gets the burst tokens?
[01:36] Diego: server-side fairshare allocator by weight. you can weight projects or give hard reservations. there's also preemption options — higher priority can preempt lower if you set that flag.
[01:47] Mei: can we do per-hour budgets? our billing expects hourly smoothing.
[01:53] Maya: yes, quota windows are flexible — per second, minute, hour, month. you can do a sliding window or fixed window; sliding windows pair better with leaky-bucket behavior.
[02:06] Sofia: can you show the console now?
[02:10] Maya: sure pulling it up. 
[02:20] [screen share noise] Diego: alright here's the org dashboard, you'll see 'quota profiles' on the left — we have a demo profile called "weekend-burst". notice the bucket size = 20k tokens, leak-rate = 2k tokens/min and a concurrency soft-limit of 50.
[02:39] Arjun: hmmm the tokens notion, is that per-request or per-token? our product disk uses variable length prompts.
[02:46] Diego: it's token-based, so larger responses consume bucket faster. we also support request-count quotas if you prefer that metric.
[02:55] Mei: in terms of enforcement, is there a hard reject or queueing? we want to avoid long tail latency.
[03:02] Diego: you can choose behaviour — immediate 429 reject, or queue up to a short window (configurable) with a priority queue. for low-latency paths we recommend soft-failover to a cheaper model rather than queueing.
[03:15] Arjun: that soft-failover, is that model-level or routing-level?
[03:20] Maya: routing-level. you set fallback chains. e.g., primary: redwood-v4-rt, fallback: redwood-v4-quant, fallback2: cached-response.
[03:29] [short crosstalk] Sofia: I like the cached-response idea for predictable cost. how do you decide what to cache?
[03:35] Diego: prefix caching for conversation starters, and KV-cache for key-value responses. Optimize can also suggest cache TTLs based on query repeat rates.
[03:45] Mei: can Optimize suggest a quantization profile balancing latency and quality?
[03:50] Diego: yep, Optimize will look at your workload distribution and recommend 8-bit or mixed-precision profiles plus batching configs.
[03:58] Arjun: security — we need KMS integration and audit logs to meet our SOC2 scope.
[04:04] Maya: we support customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS / GCP CMEK) and HSM connectors for Private deployments. audit logs are available in the Console and can be forwarded to your SIEM — we also include token-level request metadata for SLO billing reconciliation.
[04:20] Mei: is SSO available for RBAC? we have strict team RBAC rules.
[04:24] Maya: yes, SSO with SAML/SCIM provisioning, and granular RBAC for roles like admin, quota-manager, and billing.
[04:32] Sofia: curious about rate-limit headers — do you expose remaining tokens to clients?
[04:36] Diego: yes we emit standard headers X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and a custom X-Redwood-Bucket-Status for bucket fullness.
[04:46] Arjun: ok can you run a live simulation of two projects spiking?
[04:50] Diego: sure starting k6 script now, you'll see traffic generator for project-alpha and project-beta.
[05:02] [simulation audio: periodic ticks, screen shows charts]
[05:15] Diego: here you can see project-alpha consumed its burst and then soft-failed to the quant model, project-beta had reservation so it kept hitting primary. I will point out the yellow band is queueing latency.
[05:30] Mei: that yellow band peaked at 1.2s, that's ok but we want <500ms for our interactive flows.
[05:36] Diego: you can reduce queueing by increasing concurrency limit or enabling more dedicated workers for that project. another approach is to set stricter fallback to cheaper model earlier to avoid queueing.
[05:48] Arjun: is there a way to do time-of-day reservations? weekends vs weekdays?
[05:54] Maya: yes scheduled reservations — you can reserve extra capacity for e.g., weekend-burst windows and autop-run the policy during those hours.
[06:02] Sofia: and cost implications? if we reserve capacity we'll pay a flat reserved fee?
[06:08] Maya: for Dedicated/reserved capacity yes, there's a commit fee; for hosted you can configure burst slots that are billed at a premium per-second rate. we'll send pricing examples.
[06:19] Arjun: what about alerting on quota exhaustion?
[06:22] Diego: you can hook into Console alerts, webhook to PagerDuty, or consume metrics via Prometheus; we emit quota.remaining as a metric and will generate alerts when thresholds cross.
[06:33] Mei: for our compliance team, we usually run a security deep-dive. who handles that?
[06:38] Maya: our security team — I'll connect you with Priya (Redwood security) and we'll share SOC2 artifact package and ATO checklist for private deploys.
[06:47] Arjun: perfect. one more technical — concurrency: how is KV-cache shared across workers? if you scale pods, does cache warm-up cause failures?
[06:55] Diego: KV cache is sharded; we do local hot-sharding plus a global layer. cache-warmup is mitigated with prefetch policies and cold-start buffers. in practice we've seen <100ms warmup for typical workloads.
[07:09] Sofia: do you support IP allowlists or private VPC endpoints?
[07:12] Maya: yes both. private deployments can be air-gapped and we support VPC endpoints for hosted customers plus allowlists for admin APIs.
[07:21] Arjun: what about audit trail retention? we need 2 years for certain events.
[07:26] Maya: audit log retention is configurable; default 90 days, enterprise plan can extend to multi-year retention and export to S3 for long-term archival.
[07:36] Mei: any rate-limiting on embedding endpoints? our embeddings run large batch jobs.
[07:41] Diego: embeddings typically use batch quotas with size/throughput controls; you can carve a large batch window with throttled throughput so it doesn't impact realtime traffic.
[07:52] Arjun: I'm thinking pilot — can we run a controlled test with our weekend traffic sample?
[07:57] Maya: absolutely. proposed plan: 2-week pilot, Redwood provisions an org-slice with reserved burst slots and project keys mirror production. we'll instrument metrics and compare cost/latency.
[08:09] Sofia: do you have a template SLA for pilot?
[08:12] Maya: yes, I'll send a pilot SLA that covers uptime, support hours, and rollback criteria.
[08:18] Diego: also note we'll run Optimize recommendations at start to set initial batching and quantization; then tune after observed traffic.
[08:26] Mei: how invasive is instrumentation on our side? we prefer minimal code changes.
[08:30] Diego: minimal — mostly header changes for project keys and optional SDK integration. we can run the tests purely by switching keys and routing rules in the Console; no deep app change needed.
[08:41] [brief pause]
[08:45] Arjun: ok I'm sold on the feature set. some procurement questions: do you accept PO for pilot?
[08:51] Maya: yes pilot POs are fine; we'll include limited refund/credits clause based on the agreed SLA. I'll follow up with legal template.
[08:59] Sofia: competitor question — we evaluated doing this in-house last year and also looked at OpenAI rate limits; what's your advantage vs rolling our own?
[09:08] Maya: re-use of optimized runtime + the orchestration for fallback/fairshare and built-in observability. building that in-house is a lot of ops cost and the ongoing model/versioning is painful.
[09:18] Diego: also Optimize gives automated tuning which most in-house setups lack.
[09:22] Mei: any gotchas for hybrid cloud? part of our infra is on-prem.
[09:28] Maya: Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem bundles; we can run a private control plane and still offer the same quota controls locally.
[09:36] Arjun: ok great. let's recap next steps.
[09:40] Maya: recap: we'll send pricing + pilot SLA, Diego will send benchmark harness + scripts, Lytic provides traffic sample and SRE contact for security. schedule pilot kickoff for week of 21st.
[09:52] Sofia: that sounds good. thanks Maya/Diego.
[09:56] Maya: thanks everyone. we'll email notes and action items.

-- End of transcript --
